name: The Pollard Sweet Chestnut by St Mary's Church

location.address: Drive to St Mary's Church, Studley Royal deer park, Ripon HG4 3DY

access: Open to walkers. Studley Royal deer park (National Trust), entered by a pedestrian gate on the footpath from the Fountains Abbey visitor centre; the tree is on the Trust's public ancient trees walk. Deer park car park is pay and display (members free). The abbey and water garden have their own entry terms.
transport: About 4 miles (6 km) from Ripon by footpath. From the Fountains Abbey visitor centre, 15 to 20 minutes on foot. The Ripon Roweller 139 bus runs towards Markington; check current times.
story:
The National Trust's word for this sweet chestnut is a pre-18th-century pollard, which means a tree already standing before 1700, and one that was cut back at head height for its wood. That makes it older than the chestnuts on the hillside nearby in the deer park at Studley Royal, which the Trust dates to about 1710.

Pollarding was a working habit. A tree cut back above the reach of grazing animals sends up a crown of new poles, harvested every few years, and a pollard often lives far longer than a tree left alone. In a deer park the height mattered, because deer eat whatever they can reach.

The chestnut stands across the roadway from St Mary's Church, the Victorian church the Trust calls a William Burges masterpiece, so a tree already standing before 1700 and a church of the 1870s face each other over the drive. Beyond them lie the water garden and the ruins of Fountains Abbey, and a path on the Trust's ancient trees walk that passes five limes opposite Choristers House.

Everything here comes from one source, the National Trust's own walk, which is a good source but a single one. Nobody has published a girth or a sharper age. If you measure it, or know more, tell us.
how_to_recognise: You can recognise it as the pollarded sweet chestnut on the right of the drive as you walk down from the pedestrian gate. It stands across the roadway from St Mary's Church, before the Lime Avenue.
